title: No Spin Zone? Lab Device Mimics Black Hole’s Energy-Sucking Power
summary:
More than half a century ago, physicist Roger Penrose proposed that energy could be extracted from a spinning black hole. His idea: a particle entering the ergosphere — a region where spacetime is dragged by the black hole’s rotation — could split, with one piece falling in and the other escaping with more energy. Later, Yakov Zel’dovich extended this to waves. Now, researchers at the CUNY Advanced Science Research Center have brought these theories to life in a lab — without any physical rotation.

The team built a radio-frequency device whose properties change rapidly across space and time, creating the illusion of ultrafast rotation. This synthetic rotation reaches effective speeds far beyond mechanical limits. “Our approach facilitates wave-matter interaction where waves with selected rotational properties extract energy from synthetic time-engineered rotation, producing broadband selective amplification,” said principal investigator Andrea Alù.

In the experiment, a ring of electronic resonators was adjusted in a synchronized sequence, generating a traveling pattern. Although stationary, the system appeared to spin at extraordinary speed to electromagnetic waves. Waves with the right characteristics extracted energy and became amplified — replicating the Penrose-Zel’dovich process. “Waves with the appropriate rotational characteristics extracted energy from the system and became amplified,” said co-lead author Hady Moussa.

The implications stretch beyond astrophysics. Synthetic rotation can mimic motion beyond light speed, offering a platform to explore extreme physics. Potential applications include wireless communications, optics, and quantum technologies. The research, published in Nature, was supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, the National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.
why_it_matters: This experiment shows that ideas once confined to black holes can be tested on Earth, potentially leading to new technologies for faster communication or quantum devices. Understanding how to extract energy from extreme environments could inspire future energy sources.

background_read: Roger Penrose (a British physicist who later won a Nobel Prize) first proposed the energy-extraction idea in 1969, long before any experimental proof was possible. Black holes are objects so dense that not even light can escape, but Penrose realized their spin could be a source of power.

Later, Yakov Zel’dovich (a Soviet physicist known for his work in astrophysics and nuclear physics) suggested that rotating systems could amplify electromagnetic waves in a similar way. The new study, conducted at the CUNY Advanced Science Research Center in New York, is the first to demonstrate this effect in a controlled laboratory setup using an array of electronic resonators.

The research was published in Nature, one of the world’s most prestigious scientific journals, and was funded by the U.S. Department of Defense, the National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation. The experiment does not use any moving parts, only cleverly timed electrical signals to mimic extreme spin.

perspectives.description: The lab demonstration proves that a long-standing cosmic theory is real and can be controlled. It offers a new way to design amplifiers and communication tools that work more efficiently by harvesting energy from engineered rotation. This could lead to smaller, more powerful gadgets.

The device is a proof of concept, and translating it to practical, everyday applications may take decades or prove too costly. Some skeptics worry that the media overhypes such experiments, creating unrealistic expectations about free energy from black-hole-like setups.

Synthetic rotation provides a laboratory analog for astrophysical processes that cannot be directly observed. It lets physicists test predictions of general relativity and quantum theory in a safe, repeatable environment. The work is a stepping stone in basic science, not an immediate product.

Future designs could simulate motion beyond the speed of light, opening a window into physics that was previously impossible to study. If engineers can miniaturize the resonator setup, it might be integrated into future cellphones or quantum computers.
